title: B2B E-Commerce Platform Selection Framework for APAC Buyers
summary: A B2B e-commerce platform selection framework built for APAC: weighted scoring, real pricing for Shopify Plus and Adobe Commerce, payments and e-invoicing gates.
body_markdown:
**Quick Answer:** A B2B e-commerce platform selection framework scores platforms on seven weighted dimensions: commercial pricing model, account hierarchy, APAC payments and credit, tax and e-invoicing, integration depth, logistics, and total cost. Fix weights before demos, gate on local payment rails, then validate with a two-week proof of concept.


---


Most B2B platform selections fail before the first demo, because the shortlist was built from a Gartner-style feature grid written for North American distributors. A B2B e-commerce platform selection framework that works in Asia-Pacific has to start somewhere else entirely: with how your customers actually pay, how your invoices actually get accepted by a tax authority, and how a carrier in Ho Chi Minh City confirms delivery of a 40-line pallet order. Get those three right and the feature checklist mostly takes care of itself. Get them wrong and you will spend the next 18 months building the plumbing your "enterprise-ready" platform was supposed to include.


I have watched this play out from both sides — as a former HSBC VP sitting on the buying side of vendor pitches, and now as the person whose team has to make the chosen platform work across Hong Kong, Singapore, Taiwan, Malaysia and Australia. What follows is the framework we use, including the parts vendors would prefer you didn't score.


## Start With Evaluation Criteria, Not Vendor Categories


The single most useful discipline is to write your criteria before you look at a single logo. Seven dimensions cover almost every B2B commerce decision in the region.


### 1. Pricing and contract logic


B2B pricing is where consumer-first platforms break. You need to score, specifically:


- Customer-specific price lists, not just customer-group discounts
- Volume and tiered break pricing at SKU and category level
- Contract pricing with start and end dates, and fallback behaviour on expiry
- Currency-specific price books (a Taiwan dealer paying TWD should not see an FX-converted USD list)
- Minimum order quantities, order multiples, and case-pack enforcement
- Quote-to-order: can a sales rep create a quote, discount a line, route it for approval, and convert it?


*Related reading:*[Shopify Plus APAC Success Case Studies 2026: The Real Numbers](https://branch8.com/posts/shopify-plus-apac-success-case-studies-2026)


Ask vendors to show contract pricing expiring mid-cart. The failure modes are instructive.


### 2. Account hierarchy and permissions


A distributor buying group in Malaysia might have one parent entity, nine branch locations, three cost centres, and a purchasing manager who can order but not approve above a threshold. Score the platform's native company-account model: parent/child companies, multiple ship-to locations under one bill-to, per-location catalogues and price lists, spending limits, and multi-step approval chains.


*Related reading:*[Bromine Supply Chain Impact: Semiconductor APAC Risk in 2026](https://branch8.com/posts/bromine-supply-chain-impact-semiconductor-apac)


### 3. Payment and credit terms


This is the criterion global vendors score worst on in APAC. You need net-30/60/90 terms with credit limits enforced at checkout, purchase-order-number capture, partial payments, and — critically — local rails. In practice that means FPS in Hong Kong, PayNow and InvoiceNow-linked settlement in Singapore, PromptPay in Thailand, VietQR in Vietnam, DuitNow in Malaysia, and bank transfer with proof-of-payment upload almost everywhere. Card-only checkout is a non-starter for wholesale in most of the region.


*Related reading:*[Claude Opus System Prompt Changes: Implications for Automation](https://branch8.com/posts/claude-opus-system-prompt-changes-implications-order-automation)


*Related reading:*[Notion Public Page Email Data Breach Implications for APAC Teams](https://branch8.com/posts/notion-public-page-email-data-breach-implications-apac)


*Related reading:*[Salesforce Headless 360 CDP Agent Integration for APAC Retail](https://branch8.com/posts/salesforce-headless-360-cdp-agent-integration-apac-retail)


### 4. Tax, invoicing and compliance


APAC e-invoicing has moved from "coming soon" to "live and mandatory" in the space of about three years. Malaysia's LHDN MyInvois requires structured e-invoice submission with phased rollout by revenue band. Singapore's IMDA InvoiceNow network is being progressively mandated for GST-registered businesses, and Singapore GST sits at 9% since 1 January 2024 (IRAS). Taiwan requires government uniform invoice (GUI) numbering. Vietnam mandates e-invoices with tax-authority codes. Hong Kong, by contrast, has no VAT/GST at all — which means a single platform instance often has to handle both a no-tax jurisdiction and three different mandatory e-invoicing regimes.


Score this as an integration question, not a feature question: does the platform expose the order and invoice data model cleanly enough for a middleware layer or local accounting system to generate compliant documents?


### 5. Logistics and fulfilment


B2B fulfilment in APAC is rarely one carrier. Score native or partner support for SF Express and Kerry in Greater China, Ninja Van and J&T across Southeast Asia, Lalamove and GogoX for same-day pallet and bulk moves, plus Australia Post/StarTrack and Aramex for AU/NZ. Then score the harder parts: split shipments across warehouses, partial fulfilment with backorder, freight-quote-on-request, and delivery-window booking.


### 6. Integration surface and ERP alignment


Your ERP is the system of record for stock, credit and pricing. The platform's job is to expose that reliably. Score API completeness (GraphQL and REST), webhook coverage, rate limits under bulk load, bulk import/export throughput, and whether pre-built connectors exist for your ERP — SAP S/4HANA, Microsoft Dynamics 365 Business Central, NetSuite, Odoo, or a regional system like Kingdee or Yonyou.


### 7. Localisation and operating model


Traditional Chinese, Simplified Chinese, Japanese, Korean, Thai, Vietnamese and Bahasa across UI, transactional email, and admin. Then the operating question: is there implementation and support capacity in your time zone, or are you filing tickets into a US business-hours queue while your Taiwan dealers can't check out?


The context for all of this: Gartner has long projected that the majority of B2B buying interactions now happen through digital and self-service channels, and McKinsey's B2B Pulse research consistently finds B2B buyers using ten or more channels across a purchase journey. The platform is no longer a side door to your sales team. It is the counter.


## Four Platform Archetypes Worth Shortlisting


Resist the urge to compare twelve products. In APAC B2B, there are effectively four shapes of answer.


### Shopify Plus with native B2B


Shopify's B2B functionality — company accounts, company locations, catalogues, price lists, payment terms — is now native to Plus rather than an app layer. Strengths: fast implementation, low operational overhead, excellent checkout conversion, and the widest app market in commerce. It handles the D2C-plus-wholesale hybrid better than anything else, which matters for the many APAC brands running both.


Honest constraints: complex approval workflows, deep quote negotiation, and configure-price-quote for engineered products need apps or custom middleware. Checkout extensibility has improved substantially but remains more constrained than a self-hosted platform. Multi-entity tax across three e-invoicing regimes will need an integration layer.


### Adobe Commerce


Adobe Commerce (Magento) still has the deepest native B2B feature set of the mainstream platforms: company accounts, requisition lists, negotiable quotes, shared catalogues, purchase orders. If your requirement list is genuinely long and idiosyncratic, this is the platform that bends furthest without custom code.


Honest constraints: total cost of ownership. Licence plus cloud infrastructure plus a specialist development team plus upgrade cycles. Adobe's own documentation on Commerce Cloud makes clear that infrastructure sizing is part of the commercial conversation. If you don't have — or won't fund — a dedicated technical team or a long-term partner, Adobe becomes expensive slowly and then suddenly.


### SHOPLINE (and regional SaaS)


For businesses whose revenue is concentrated in Greater China and Southeast Asia, regional platforms deserve a genuine slot on the shortlist rather than a courtesy mention. SHOPLINE's advantage is not feature depth against Adobe; it is that local payment rails, Traditional Chinese admin, WhatsApp and LINE commerce integration, and regional logistics come pre-wired rather than as a six-week integration project. Constraint: a smaller third-party app market, and less headroom if you later need to operate at scale in the US or EU.


### Composable / headless


commercetools, BigCommerce Enterprise with a headless front end, or a Shopify-headless build. The case for composable is real when you have multiple brands and geographies sharing one catalogue and pricing engine, or when commerce has to be embedded into a portal, a dealer app, and a marketplace feed simultaneously.


Honest constraints: you are buying a platform and taking on the responsibility of an in-house product team. Front end, CMS, search, and orchestration are now yours to maintain. Composable is the correct answer far less often than the marketing suggests — usually when annual GMV and organisational maturity both justify a standing engineering function.

## Pricing: Real Numbers and Where the Money Actually Goes


Licence cost is the number executives ask for and the least useful number in the decision. Here is what is publicly verifiable and what is directionally reliable.


### Published licence pricing


**Shopify Plus** is listed on Shopify's own pricing page at USD 2,300 per month on a three-year term, or USD 2,500 per month billed monthly, with variable-fee pricing available for merchants above roughly USD 800,000 monthly volume. Payment processing is separate; Shopify Payments rates vary by market, and non-Shopify-Payments gateways attract an additional platform fee.


**BigCommerce Enterprise** is quote-based; the company publishes lower tiers openly and enterprise plans are typically negotiated in the low-to-mid five figures annually depending on order volume and API needs.


**Adobe Commerce** does not publish licence pricing. Implementation partners across the market consistently describe tiered annual licensing scaled to gross merchandise value, commonly cited in the range of USD 20,000 to well over USD 100,000 per year, with Commerce Cloud infrastructure billed on top. Treat any specific figure you see online — including that range — as an anchor for your own RFQ, not a quote.


**commercetools** is quote-based and consumption-influenced. Public sector procurement records and analyst commentary put enterprise contracts firmly in six figures annually. It is not a mid-market price point.


### The costs that actually decide TCO


In our experience implementing B2B commerce for listed retail groups, catering operators and dealer-network manufacturers across the region, licence is rarely more than 20–30% of three-year spend. The rest:


- **Implementation.** Scope-driven. A Shopify Plus B2B build with ERP integration and two local payment gateways is a different order of magnitude from an Adobe Commerce multi-entity rollout across four markets.
- **ERP and middleware.** Almost always underestimated. Pricing sync, credit-limit checks, stock availability by warehouse, and order write-back are four separate pieces of work, each with its own error-handling requirements.
- **E-invoicing compliance.** Budget per market. MyInvois in Malaysia, InvoiceNow in Singapore, GUI in Taiwan, and Vietnam's coded e-invoices are four distinct integrations, not one.
- **Payment gateway work.** Local rails (FPS, PayNow, DuitNow, PromptPay, VietQR) plus a bank-transfer reconciliation flow.
- **Data migration.** Customer hierarchies, historical orders, contract prices. B2B data is dirtier than D2C data because it has lived in spreadsheets.
- **Run cost.** Hosting (Adobe/composable), monitoring, security patching, and a change budget. Assume 15–25% of implementation cost annually for continuous improvement, or the platform ossifies.


The honest framing: SaaS platforms move cost from capex to opex and from your team to the vendor's. Self-hosted and composable platforms give you control and hand you the payroll. Neither is cheaper in the abstract. It depends entirely on whether you have, or want, engineers.


## A Weighted Scoring Framework You Can Run in a Week


Here is the scoring model. Score each platform 0–5 on every dimension, multiply by weight, total to 100. The weights below are a starting point for a mid-market APAC B2B business selling through dealers or distributors — adjust them, but adjust them *before* you see the scores.


### The seven dimensions and default weights


- **B2B commercial model — 20 points.** Price lists, contract pricing, MOQs, quotes, approvals.
- **Account hierarchy and self-service — 15 points.** Company accounts, multi-location, roles, reordering, order history, credit visibility.
- **APAC payments and credit — 15 points.** Local rails, terms enforcement, PO capture, reconciliation.
- **Tax and e-invoicing readiness — 10 points.** Multi-entity, multi-jurisdiction, integration surface for MyInvois/InvoiceNow/GUI.
- **Integration and data — 15 points.** API depth, rate limits, bulk throughput, ERP connectors, webhook reliability.
- **Logistics and fulfilment — 10 points.** Regional carriers, split/partial shipment, freight quoting.
- **Total cost and operating fit — 15 points.** Three-year TCO, in-region support, partner availability, internal skills match.


### Scoring rules that keep the exercise honest


1. **Score only what you have seen work.** A roadmap commitment scores 1, not 4. Write the demo date next to every score.
2. **Use a hard gate before weighting.** If a platform cannot enforce a credit limit at checkout or cannot support your primary local payment rail without a custom build, it fails the gate regardless of total score.
3. **Score the partner separately.** Platform and implementation partner are two decisions. A strong platform with no in-region delivery capacity is a slower project than a mid-tier platform with a team in your time zone.
4. **Force a spread.** If every platform scores 3 on a dimension, your criterion is too vague to be useful. Rewrite it as a testable statement.


### Two worked weighting variants


**Dealer-network manufacturer (AU/NZ plus SEA):** shift 5 points from Logistics into B2B commercial model. Quote negotiation, contract pricing and approval chains dominate; parcel logistics matters less than freight quoting.


**Multi-brand retail group running D2C and wholesale (HK/TW/SG):** shift 5 points from Tax into Integration and Total cost. One platform serving two very different order profiles makes API throughput and unified inventory the binding constraint.


This is the part people search for as a "B2B e-commerce platform selection framework template" or PDF. The template matters far less than the discipline of fixing weights before scoring — that one rule removes most of the post-hoc rationalisation from platform decisions.

## Test the Platform, Don't Watch the Demo


Every vendor demo is a happy path. The only reliable evaluation method is a two-week paid or sandboxed proof of concept against your own data. Three tests separate platforms quickly.


**Test 1: Contract pricing under a real catalogue.** Load 5,000 SKUs and three customer-specific price lists with overlapping volume breaks. Then query a price as a specific company location. On Shopify's B2B model, this is a direct API question:


```text
1  query CompanyLocationCatalog($locationId: ID!) {    2    companyLocation(id: $locationId) {    3      name    4      buyerExperienceConfiguration { paymentTermsTemplate { name } }    5      catalogs(first: 5) {    6        edges { node {    7          title    8          priceList { currency parent { adjustment { type value } } }    9        } }    10      }    11    }    12  }
```


If the answer requires three round trips and a cache, note that — it is your product-listing page latency.


**Test 2: Bulk order throughput.** Submit a 500-line order via API and measure response time and error handling. Then run a 20,000-SKU price update and watch the rate limits:


```text
1  curl -s -D - -o /dev/null \    2    -H "X-Shopify-Access-Token: $TOKEN" \    3    -H "Content-Type: application/json" \    4    -X POST "https://$SHOP.myshopify.com/admin/api/2025-01/graphql.json" \    5    -d @bulk-price-update.json | grep -i 'x-shopify-shop-api-call-limit'
```


**Test 3: The e-invoice round trip.** Take one order and produce a compliant document for your hardest market. For Malaysia, that means mapping your order to the MyInvois payload and submitting it — the field mapping exercise alone will tell you whether the platform's data model gives you supplier TIN, buyer TIN, SST registration and classification codes without custom fields bolted on.


One pattern worth naming: on a project for a manufacturer selling through a regional dealer network, the deciding factor between two otherwise close platforms wasn't a listed feature at all. It was that one platform's order object could carry dealer-specific freight terms and a PO reference through to the ERP without a custom extension, and the other needed a metafield scheme and a webhook to do the same job. That difference showed up in a two-day proof of concept and would have been invisible in a demo.


## How to Evaluate: Running the Framework End to End


A workable B2B e-commerce platform selection framework runs on a six-week clock, not a six-month one.


**Week 1 — Fix the requirements and the weights.** Interview three sales reps, two customer-service staff, your finance controller and two actual customers. Write the requirement list. Set the seven weights and get the CFO and head of sales to sign them. Do not proceed until weights are signed.


**Week 2 — Define hard gates and shortlist.** Three to four platforms maximum, drawn from the four archetypes. Gate on payments, credit terms, e-invoicing surface and in-region support before anything else.


**Weeks 3–4 — Demos against your scenarios.** Send each vendor the same five scenarios in advance: a contract-priced multi-location order, a quote requiring approval, a partial shipment, a credit-limit rejection, and a tax-compliant invoice for your hardest market. Score live, in the room, on the shared sheet.


**Week 5 — Proof of concept.** Two finalists, real data, the three tests above. This is where you also test the partner: how fast do they respond, how honest are they about what doesn't work?


**Week 6 — Total cost and decision.** Build three-year TCO for both finalists including implementation, integration, compliance, run cost and change budget. Present scores and TCO together. If the higher-scoring platform costs 60% more over three years, that trade-off is a board conversation, not a procurement one — and it should be stated plainly rather than buried.

## What to Do Monday Morning


1. **Write your seven weights and circulate them for sign-off.** Twenty minutes of work that prevents the most common failure in platform selection: criteria drifting to match the vendor you already liked.
2. **List every payment method and tax jurisdiction you invoice in today.** Then check each shortlisted platform's documentation for native support. Anything not natively supported is a line item in your integration budget, not a footnote.
3. **Book one hour with your finance controller on credit and reconciliation.** How terms are set, how limits are enforced, how bank transfers are matched today. This conversation reshapes more shortlists than any feature comparison.
